sections.text: Acknowledgment 'The Compendium on Kerala High Court Procedure' is prepared by the Kerala Judicial Academy as desired by the Hon’ble Mr. Justice S. Manikumar, Chief Justice, High Court of Kerala under the guidance of the Hon'ble President and members of the Board of Governors of the Kerala Judicial Academy. The preparation of the compendium was monitored by the Committee comprising of the Hon'ble Mr. Justice Sunil Thomas and the Hon'ble Mr. Justice V.G. Arun, Judges of the High Court of Kerala and members of the Board of Governors, Kerala Judicial Academy, Director, Kerala Judicial Academy, and the Registrar (Judicial), High Court of Kerala. The Academy expresses thanks and gratitude to the Hon'ble the Chief Justice, High Court of Kerala, Hon’ble Mr. Justice S.V. Bhatti, Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sunil Thomas, Hon’ble Mrs. Justice Anu Sivaraman, Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sathish Ninan and Hon’ble Mr. Justice V.G. Arun, Judges of the High Court of Kerala and the President and members respectively of the Board of Governors of the Kerala Judicial Academy, Hon'ble Mr. Justice A. Hariprasad, former Judge, High Court of Kerala and former President, Board of Governors, Kerala Judicial Academy for the valuable guidance and support given by them in the preparation of this compendium. This compendium is an output of the tireless work put forth by the members of the Sub- Committee constituted for this purpose. The Academy is thankful to Advocate G. Unnikrishnan, Convenor, Advocate Parvathi Menon, Advocate Hariraj M.R., and Sri. Valsaraj P.C. Filing Scrutiny Officer, High Court of Kerala, members of the Sub-Committee. who have put in a lot of time and effort to give shape to the compendium. The contribution and support provided by the lawyers and officers and staff of the High Court of Kerala is acknowledged and remembered with gratitude. K. Sathyan, Director Kerala Judicial Academy

sections.text: Message KERALAJUDICIALACADEMY ATHANI,ERNAKULAMDist.683585 PhoneOffice:04842476310 e-mail:kjakhc@gmail.com 10.3.2022 A High Court exercises jurisdiction in respect of various cases institutedbefore it.There are legislations indicating the procedure tobe followed. The need to have a single window document containing all minute details of the procedure followed was mooted by the Hon'ble Mr. Justice S.Manikumar, Chief Justice,High Court of Kerala entrusted the work to the Kerala Judicial Academy. The activities of the Kerala Judicial Academy are not limited to imparting judicial education. It is engaged in training other stakeholders in the justice delivery system also. The Academy also conducts legal research on topics relevant to the judiciary.Therefore,a Sub-Committee was constituted byincluding lawyers and staff of the High Court competentto contribute to the preparation of the Compendium.They have done a wonderful job by preparing the Compendium of the Kerala High Court Procedure. The Sub-Committee deserves special mentionfor the meritoriouswork done by them under the convenorship ofAdvocate G.Unnikrishnan.

sections.text: CHAPTER I - INTRODUCTION [1] The procedure for filing a case in the High Court is mainly governed by the Kerala High Court Act, 1958 [hereinafter referred to as the “Act”] and the Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971 [hereinafter referred to as the “Rules”]. The “Act” and the “Rules” of the High Court are exhaustive in nature. The “Act” and the “Rules” are in addition to the various Acts, Codes and Rules which are supplemental to the filing of a case before the High Court. This hand book serves as a guide and covers the various types of cases filed in the High Court, important Sections and Rules which helps a lawyer in filing a case before the High Court. [2] Chapter X of this handbook gives the table of nomenclature of cases filed in the High Court. The important provisions of the “Rules”, the Court Fees payable, the period of Limitation applicable for each type of cases and relevant details in connection with that particular nomenclature case are mentioned in the chapters dealing with each type of cases. The Forms prescribed under the “Rules” which find a mention in the handbook are also provided in Chapter XXIII of this handbook. [3] Chapter XV of the “Rules” provide the procedure to be followed when the cases are received/filed before the High Court under Section 21 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. Prior to the Chartered Accounts [Amendment] Act, 2006 the High Court was vested with certain powers under Sections 21 and 22A of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. By virtue of the Chartered Accountants [Amendment] Act, 2006 the existing Sections 21 and 22A were substituted with new Sections 21 and 22A whereby the powers exercised by the High Court were abolished. The Amendment Act, 2006 also provided for a transitional provision whereby any reference or appeal made to the High Court prior to the commencement of the Amendment Act 2006 continued to be governed by the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act 1949, as if the Chartered Accountants Act 1949 had not been amended by the Amendment Act. [4] Chapter XIX of the “Rules” provide the procedure to be followed when a Reference under Section 21 or an Appeal or Revision under 30 of the Company Secretaries Act, 1980 were filed. Prior to the Company Secretaries (Amendment) Act, 2006 the High Court was vested with certain powers under Sections 21 and 30 of the Company Secretaries Act, 1980. By virtue of the Company Secretaries (Amendment) Act, 2006, the existing Section 21 was substituted with new Section 21 and Section 30 was omitted, whereby the powers exercised by the High Court were abolished. The Amendment Act, 2006 also provided for a transitional provision whereby any reference or appeal made to a High Court prior to the commencement of the Amendment Act, 2006 continued to be governed by the provisions of the Company Secretaries Act, 1980, as if the Company Secretaries Act, 1980 had not been amended by the Amendment Act. [5] The High Court has also enacted the Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala) 2021for filing of cases through electronic mode as part of the efforts to employ technology to expediate court proceedings. The salient rules regarding the same are mentioned in Chapter V of this book. [6] This book will be a ready reckoner for Judges, Judicial Officers, Lawyers, Registry of the High Court, Advocate Clerks, and all concerned on the High court procedure. **********************

CHAPTER II - CONSTITUTION AND POWERS OF BENCHES [1] The powers of a Single Judge, Bench of two Judges and Vacation Judge are provided in Section 3, 4 and 8 of the “Act”. Section 3 Powers of Single Judge. - The powers of the High Court in relation to the following matters may be exercised by a Single Judge, provided that the Judge before whom the matter is posted for hearing may adjourn it for being heard and determined by a Bench of two Judges:-
(1) Determining in which of several Courts having jurisdiction a suit shall be heard.
(2) Admission of an appeal in forma pauperis.
(3) Exercise of original jurisdiction under any law for the time being in force.
(4) Exercise of the powers under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and under Section 22 of the Kerala Small Cause Courts Act, 1957
(5) Any matter of an interlocutory character in appeals and other proceedings.
(6) Admission of an appeal presented after the expiry of the period allowed by the law of limitation.
(7) Admission of an appeal from the judgment or order of any Criminal Court
(8) Exercise of the power to revise the proceedings of any Criminal Court:
Provided that in the exercise of such power a Single Judge shall not impose a sentence of death or imprisonment for life.
(9) Exercise of the powers conferred by Section 426 and 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
(10) Exercise of the powers under –
(i) Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908;
(ii) Sections 526 and 526A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898;
(iii) Clause (1) of Article 226 of the Constitution of India except were such power relates to the issue of a writ of the nature of Habeas Corpus, and
(iv) Articles 227 and 228 of the Constitution of India.
(11) Exercise of the power under sub-section (2) of Section 19 of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957.
(12) A report under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898
(13) An appeal –
(a) from a judgment or order of a Criminal Court, except in cases in which the appellant or a person tried with him has been sentenced to death or imprisonment for life.
Provided that in the exercise of such power a Single Judge shall not impose a sentence of death or imprisonment for life;

(e) from an appellate decree or order;
(f) under Section 79(3) of the Insolvency Act, 1955; and
(g) under Section 476B of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898;
(h) from an award passed by a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. CHAPTER III - VAKALATH AND POWER OF ATTORNEY A. VAKALATH [1] Chapter II of the “Rules” – Rule 17 to Rule 31 - deals with Advocates and their Registered Clerks. The said chapter also deals with the Vakalath filed in the High Court. The relevant rules which deal with Vakalath are Rules 17; 18; 19; 20; 21; 22 and 24. They are extracted below for ready reference: Production of Vakalath. - (1) No Advocate shall be entitled to act in any proceeding, unless he files a Vakalath.
Provided that where an Advocate already on record in any proceeding appoints another Advocate to appear for him at the hearing of the case, it shall not be necessary for the latter to file a Vakalath:
Provided further that an Advocate appearing for an accused person in a criminal proceeding may, instead of filing a Vakalath, file a memorandum of appearance containing declaration that he has been duly instructed to appear by/or on behalf of the accused.
(2) An Advocate appearing on behalf of the Central or State Government or on behalf of any public servant sued or suing in his official capacity shall be required to file only a memorandum of appearance. Particulars in the memorandum. - The memorandum of appearance referred to in the preceding rule shall contain the name and address of the Advocate, roll number, the number and year of the proceedings, the names of the parties to the same and the name and position in the proceeding of the party for whom the Advocate appears. Form and attestation of vakalath. - (1) Every Vakalath shall, unless otherwise permitted by the Court, be in Form No.1 and may authorise the Advocate to appear in subsequent proceedings such as applications for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, appeals to a Division Bench etc. The name of the Advocate or the Advocate’s if more than one Advocate, is appointed, shall be inserted in the Vakalath before it is executed. It shall be dated at the time of its execution and of its acceptance. Its execution shall be attested by a Judicial Officer, a District Registrar, a Sub Registrar, the Chief Ministerial Officer of a Civil or Criminal Court in the State of Kerala, a member of Parliament or of the Legislature of any State in India, the Mayor, Chairman, President, Executive Authority or member of any Municipal Corporation, or Municipal Council, or other Local Authority in India, a Village Officer, a Gazetted Officer serving in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State in India, a Commissioned Officer in the Defence Forces of India, an Ambassador or Envoy duly accredited by or to the Central Government or an Advocate other than the Advocate accepting the vakalath:
Provided that any other person may attest the vakalath where the executant is personally known to the Advocate in whose favour the vakalath is executed and where the executant signs the same in the presence of the Advocate and an endorsement is made by the Advocate to the above effect.
(2) The authority attesting the vakalath under sub-rule (1) shall certify that it has been duly executed in his presence and subscribe his signature over his name and designation. No vakalath shall be attested unless the Advocate’s name is inserted therein previous to its execution. When vakalath is executed by a party who appears to the person before whom it is executed to be illiterate, blind or unacquainted with the language in which the vakalath is written, the person shall certify that the vakalath was read, translated and explained in his presence to the executant, that he seemed to understand it and that he made his signature or thumb mark in his presence.
(3) The execution of a vakalath by a person in custody may be authenticated by the Jailor, Station House Officer or other Office in Charge.
(4) The execution of vakalath other than those covered by sub-rule (3) shall be made in the presence of at least one witness. When a registered clerk signs as witness to the execution of a vakalath, he shall affix his full signature and legibly write his name along with register number allotted to him from the Registry of the High Court.
(5) Every vakalath shall contain an endorsement of the Advocate in whose favour it is executed that it has been accepted by him. There shall also be endorsed on the vakalath a statement of his

The following guidelines are issued regarding the notification of appointment of Standing Counsel by various institutions for conducting cases in the High Court.
1. The institutions coming under the head ‘Government’ appended as Annexure I to the circular shall be allowed to designate their Standing Counsel. Such Standing Counsel can enter appearance by filing memo of appearance.
2. The institutions coming under the definition of State (Statutory Bodies, Public Sector Companies, Nationalized Banks, Universities etc. shall be allowed to appoint Standing Counsel but hereafter they shall file vakalath in the cases in which they appear.

The institutions in Annexure III appended to the circular are eschewed from the list of Standing Counsel maintained by the High Court as these institutions do not come under the definition of ‘Government’/’State’. Hereafter, any counsel entering appearance on behalf of these institutions shall do so by filing a vakalath. However, those Advocates who have already entered appearance in a pending case on behalf of these institutions by filing memo can continue to appear till the disposal of that case. Hereafter, the High Court will not consider any request to notify Standing Counsel on behalf of the institutions which do not come under the definition of ‘Government’/’State’.

The High Court in future, shall notify the Standing Counsel only in respect of those institutions’ either coming under the head Government or under the definition of State (Public Sector Companies, Nationalized Banks, Statutory bodies, Universities, etc.) The Government and its officers alone (as per Annexure I), as per Rule 17(2) of the “Rules” are entitled to file memo of appearance and all others shall vakalath.
5. The institutions while intimating the High Court the name of its Standing Counsel shall indicate the office address of the Standing Counsel at Ernakulam.
6. Even though an institution in the Annexures I and II can engage any lawyer/panel of lawyers apart from the designated Standing Counsel to conduct their cases by filing memo of appearance/vakalath, the High Court shall not notify the names of such lawyers/panel of lawyers. The High Court shall notify only one Standing Counsel for each institution and he alone will have the right to receive advance copy of the petition. POWER-OF-ATTORNEY [1] The Case Laws & Instructions issued regarding the filing of power-of-attorney are mentioned below. Case Laws: Appearance by a Power-of-Attorney holder: An appearance, application or act in any Court or to any Court can be effectively made or done by a party either he himself or by his power of attorney holder. Sethi P.V. & another v Nil ILR 2021(2) Ker 125 DB Memo is to be filed to record the appearance of a party through the Power-of-Attorney in the cause title of the appeal - Insistence on a memo is on account of many practical problems encountered by the Registry while drafting decrees and also in making the case records straight. We do not find any reason from Rule 22 of the Civil Rules of Practice to hold that a memo accompanying a power-of-attorney shall not be insisted or any bar in insisting on it. The rule of procedure shall be interpreted not only to suit the convenience of the parties, but to attain clarity and accuracy in the proceedings. Therefore, we find a legal logic in the insistence on the part of the Registry to submit a memo along with the power-of-attorney. Order of Hon’ble Sri.Justice A.Hariprasad & Hon’ble Sri.Justice P.V.Kunhikrishnan dt. 3.2.2021 in M.F.A[Forest]114/2018 P.O.A not authorising to file Writ Petition - Registry noted defect on the ground that the power of attorney does not authorise the agent to file a writ petition in the High Court and that it only authorises him to file a case in the civil courts. The Bench held that the High Court is also a civil court and that the relief sought is in respect of the immovable property mentioned in the power-of-attorney and therefore the objection of the Registry was overruled Order of Hon’ble Sri.Justice P.N.Ravindran & Hon’ble Sri.Justice P.Somarajan dt.3.4.2017 in unnumbered W.P.(C)[ZW.P.(C)265 of 17] Official Memorandum Filing of memo to record in the cause title the appearance of a party through Power-of Attorney When the respondent in the party array who is not represented by Power of Attorney in the cause title of the appeal, subsequently engages a counsel and files vakalath on his behalf through a Power of Attorney, no steps are taken by the counsel, to get the Power of Attorney recorded in the cause title and thus the cause title remains unchanged.

sections.title: Similarly, when a counsel appearing for the appellant/respondent relinquishes...
sections.text: Similarly, when a counsel appearing for the appellant/respondent relinquishes vakalath and the party engages a fresh counsel through a Power of Attorney, the same is not recorded in the cause title. Moreover, when the appeals are referred for mediation and the parties appear through their Power of Attorney in the Mediation Centre/Adalat and the mediation settlement agreement/compromise are entered into by the Power-of-Attorney, the same is not recorded in the appeal and consequently in the cause title of the judgment. This causes procedural difficulties to the Decree Section, while drafting decrees. The Hon’ble the Chief Justice, having considered the above facts, has directed that necessary instructions be issued, to insist on filing of memo to record, in the cause title of the appeal, the appearance of a party through his Power of Attorney, as specified in Rule 22 of the Civil Rules of Practice. The Filing Section is hereby instructed to ensure that a memo to record the appearance of a party through the Power of Attorney in the cause title of the appeal is necessarily filed in such case. Official Memorandum No.A1-27543/14 dt.13.08.2014 issued by the High Court Instructions to Registry regarding the verification of Power-of-Attorney Where the party represents through the Power-of-Attorney Holder, the Examiner should verify the original Powerof-Attorney and make an endorsement in the order sheet that he has verified the original Power-of Attorney and returned the same. The Examiners should also ensure that a certified copy of the original power- of=attorney has been produced and kept with the case records for the record of the High Court. If the Original Power-of-Attorney is not produced on the ground that it has been produced in the lower Court, the party must produce certified copy and the same shall not be returned. Instructions of Registrar (Judicial) dt.12.3.12 Court Fee to be affixed while producing Power-of-Attorney Court fee of Rs.10/- under Schedule II Article 15 of the Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959 to be affixed. *****************

sections.title: CHAPTER IV - FORM AND INSTITUTION OF PROCEEDINGS [1] Chapter III of the “Rules”...
sections.text:
CHAPTER IV - FORM AND INSTITUTION OF PROCEEDINGS [1] Chapter III of the “Rules” – Rule 32 to Rule 50 - prescribes the procedure as to how each proceeding is to be instituted in the High Court. The important rules that are to be followed in respect of individual types of cases are extracted in the respective chapters dealing with such cases. The following are the relevant general rules applicable to all types of proceedings. Rule 5(7A) Rule 5(7B) Electronic Filing (e-filing) means the electronic transmission of petitions, appeals and other proceedings to the court using the court’s electronic filing system. Electronic Payment (e-payment) means all payments into court and out of court made through electronic means. Presentation of proceedings. – (1) All petitions, appeals and other proceedings shall be presented in person by the party, or his Advocate or the Advocate’s registered clerk or by electronic filing (e-filing).
(2) The Chief Justice may from time to time issue practice directions for electronic filing of the category of cases and the said directions shall be effective from the dates as may be notified. Papers sent by post. - Unless the Court otherwise orders, no document required to be presented to or filed into Court which is sent by post or by telegram shall be received or filed into Court. Form of Proceedings. - (1) All petitions, affidavits, memoranda of appeal and other proceedings presented to the court shall be typewritten or printed on one side, fairly and legibly, on stamp paper or on white foolscap folio paper with an outer margin of about 4 cm and an inner margin of about 1.5 cm. Numbers shall be expressed in figures. ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………. . All petitions, affidavits, memoranda of appeal and other proceedings presented before the High Court shall be in A4 size papers and typewritten/printed on both sides. Official Memorandum D1-1/104010/2019 dt.22.9.2020 .................................................................................................................................................................................................................................. As per Rule 5 of Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala), 2021, pleadings are to be in A4 size paper, Font to be in Times New Roman 14 point, all text with 1.5 Line Space, Alignment must be ‘justified’, Top, Bottom, Left and Right Margins are to be 1.5”, 1.5 “, 1.75 “, and 1.0 “in respectively. Any document typed in Local Language are to be in Unicode Font 12. ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………
(2) All main proceedings such as Writ Petitions, Writ Appeals, Contempt Petitions, Civil and Criminal Appeal Memoranda, Revision Petitions etc. shall be presented to the Court with thick covering sheets of thick durable paper bearing protected holes at the top and bottom left-hand corner one inch apart from the outer edges, placed at the top and bottom.
(3) All proceedings shall be presented in book form without folding, neatly stitched in one bunch on the left margin and the pages therein shall be consecutively numbered. In the main proceedings, the thick covering sheets at the top and bottom shall be left unstitched and shall be tied together with other papers by passing removable tags through the holes at the top and bottom left-hand corners. The entire case file proceedings shall further be tied across using white tape.
(4) All main proceedings shall contain an index sheet placed immediately below the covering sheet, setting forth the brief description of the contents therein with reference to the respective page numbers. One blank sheet shall be placed below the index sheet for making further entries.
(5) A synopsis containing the dates and events chronologically arranged points to be urged, Acts/Rules to be referred and authorities to be cited shall be filed along with all main proceedings and shall be placed below the blank sheet.
(6) Miscellaneous petitions filed along with main proceedings shall be placed immediately before the covering sheet at the bottom of the main proceedings and shall be flagged noting “IA No….”

sections.title: Rule45 A (7) Miscellaneous petitions and pleadings filed in pending cases shall...
sections.text:
Rule45 A
(7) Miscellaneous petitions and pleadings filed in pending cases shall be flagged noting thereon “IA No….”/brief description of pleadings such as “Counter by R…/ Reply by R…../ Statement by ……” etc. Statement regarding value of the Appeal etc.- Every Memorandum of Appeal or objection and every application for review shall contain a statement of the value of the appeal or objection and the value of the suit or proceeding giving rise to the appeal, for the purpose of court fee and jurisdiction. Every Revision Petition shall state the value of the suit or other proceeding from which it arises. The section of the Court Fees Act under which the appeal, petition or other proceeding falls shall also be stated. Date and Signature. - (1) Whenever under the Code or under these rules or any other law for the time being in force, any proceeding filed in court has to be signed by any party, he shall subscribe his name beneath or against his signature:
Provided that when the signature consists of his name, it is not necessary that the name should be repeated, but if the name be not easily decipherable from the signature the name should be legibly written.
(2) Every proceeding filed in court shall be dated the day it is signed as also the day it is presented in Court. Docketing. - All proceedings and other documents filed in Court shall be docketed on the fact of the covering sheet placed at the top endorsing the name of the Court, the number and year of the proceeding to which it relates, the name of the person presenting the same and the date of presentation in Court. In addition to the above particulars, in the case of a memorandum of appeal or petition, an abbreviated cause title and short description of its contents shall also be given in the docket in Form No.2:
Provided that the docketing for main proceedings such as Original Petition, Civil and Criminal Appeal Memorandum, Revision Petitions etc. shall be on thick durable paper, preferably Maplitho or Double Crown Paper Revision Petitions. - When no period of limitation is prescribed by any other law, a Revision Petition shall be presented within 90 days of the order complained of. The provisions of Sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963, shall apply to such petitions. Papers to accompany Revision Petitions.- A Revision Petition shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order or decree sought to be revised, a certified copy of the judgment, if any, on which the decree or order is based, a certified copy of the judgment or order, if any, of the court or tribunal of the first instance, one additional set of typewritten or printed copies of the judgments and orders above-mentioned, by as many authenticated copies of the Revision Petition as there are respondents, two additional copies of the same for the use of the court and the fees prescribed for service of notice with the particulars thereof. Petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.- All petitions under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 shall be accompanied by a copy of the proceeding against which the petition is directed, certified as true by the Advocate of the petitioner or by the petitioner when the petition is filed in person.
Explanation: - The expression ‘proceeding’ shall include complaint, F.I.R., charge or order as the case may be.
(1) Certain provisions of the Code to apply to Civil Revision Petitions. - The provisions of Rules 11(2), 17,18,19 and 21 of Order XLI of the Code as modified by Order XLIA shall apply mutatis mutandis to Civil Revision Petitions.
(2) Provisions regarding abatement. - The provisions of Order XXII of the Code and the Limitation Act, 1963 relating to abatement shall apply to Civil Revision Petitions. Statement of facts. - The memorandum in Second Appeals, Civil Miscellaneous Appeals and Civil Revision Petitions shall contain a brief statement of the facts of the case and shall set forth the grounds of objection to the judgment or order appealed against or sought to be revised. Matters requiring admission. - Notwithstanding anything in Rules 41,45 and 148 in matters which require orders admitting the same, the copies to be produced for service on the respondents and the fees for service of notice may be presented within seven days of the order admitting the matter:

sections.title: Rule 50A Rule 50B Provided that any interim order passed in the case shall not...
sections.text:
Rule 50A Rule 50B
Provided that any interim order passed in the case shall not be communicated to the concerned Court or tribunal or the respondents, until the process fees and the necessary papers have been filed for service on the respondents, both in the main and in the interlocutory manner. Name of the Pleader in the Subordinate Court to be stated. - Every proceeding instituted prior to the disposal of the main proceedings in a Subordinate Court shall mentions, as far as possible, the names and address of the Pleaders, if any, who represented the opposite parties in the Subordinate Court for effecting service under Rule 59. Return of papers in improper language etc.- All papers which are couched in improper language or are illegible or are unnecessary prolix shall be returned for rectification.
Explanation. - Papers written in pencil shall be deemed to be illegible for the purpose of this rule, unless they be the originals received by the party. Electronic Payments. - Payments into court and out of court shall be made by the method of electronic payment (e-payment) Chief Justice to issue directions. - The Chief Justice may from time to time issue practice directions for electronic payment of the category of cases and the said directions shall be effective from the dates as may be notified. Application how made. - An application with respect to any of the matters mentioned in these rules shall be made by a petition to the Court stating the relief sought and the order prayed for and the provisions of law under which it is sought. Any evidence thereon shall be given by affidavit. Case Law: Every Petition to be supported by Affidavit. - When multiple petitions are filed in a case, each one should be supported by a separate affidavit to ensure the facts and the practice of filing a single affidavit as evidence for more than one petition should not be entertained. Registry directed to ensure that. Sadanandan Nair & others v Sree Perumanpura Devaswom & another 2017 KHC 4856 Notification: Full Postal Address in all proceedings – The actual postal address of the parties, with the correct PIN Code, shall be shown in all proceedings filed in the High Court and no proceedings will be received without such actual postal address. Notification No.A1-14065/2007 dt.09.10.07 issued by the High Court [2] Rules Regarding Appeals The following general rules of the “Rules” govern the appeals that are filed in the High Court of Kerala. Papers to be filed with memoranda of appeals. - Every memorandum of appeal shall be accompanied by the following documents, namely. -
(a) Certified copy of the judgment or order appealed against.
(b) Duly authenticated copy of petition, affidavit including reply affidavit and annexures thereto, in the case of Company Appeals.
(c) Duly authenticated copy of the writ petition/Original Petition, affidavits including counter and reply affidavits’ and statements, if any, filed in the Writ Petition/Original Petition and annexures thereto, in the case of Writ Appeals filed, in which urgent memos are filed along with it or within one month of its institution and Writ Appeals filed against interim orders in pending Writ Petitions/Original Petition.
(d) As many clear authenticated copies of the memorandum of appeal as there are respondents to be served, two additional copies with the documents mentioned in the clauses (a), (b) and (c) for the use of the Court and in appeals where the State is a respondent, two more copies for the use of that respondent.
(e) Such papers as are referred to in the Code with regard to appeals.
(f) The fees prescribed for service of notice on respondent
(g) The particulars for service as set out in Form No.3.

sections.title: Provided that in the case of a Memorandum of Appeal presented after the...
sections.text:
Provided that in the case of a Memorandum of Appeal presented after the expiration of time limited by law, or memorandum of appeal presented in forma pauperis; the fees for the service of notice of the appeal may be paid within seven days of the final order of the Court excusing the delay or granting leave to file the said proceeding in forma pauperis, as the case may be;
Provided further that one of the additional copies filed for use of the Court shall be in ledger paper. Appeals barred by limitation.- Every Memorandum of Appeal or other proceeding which is presented after the expiration of the time limited by law, shall be accompanied by a petition to excuse the delay and as many copies thereof as there are respondents to be served and by two additional copies for the use of the court, by the fees prescribed for service of notice of the petition on the respondents and by the particulars for service as in Form No.3. Appeals under Section 5 of the High Court Act. - (1) When an appeal against an appellate decree or order has been disposed of by Single Judge an application for a declaration that the case is a fit one for further appeal under Section 5 of the Kerala High Court, 1959, may be made orally immediately after the judgment is delivered.
(2) If no oral application is made as aforesaid a written application may be made within 15 days from the date of the judgment. Such application shall be accompanied by a copy of the judgment.
(3) The application shall be posted before the Judge who passed the judgment and he may, after hearing the applicant or his Advocate, either allow or dismiss the application.
(4) Where the application is granted, the applicant shall present the appeal together with a copy of the order granting the application within 30 days from the date of the order.
(5) The provisions of Orders XLI and XLIA of the Code shall apply, as far as may be, to appeals presented under this rule.
(6) The provisions of Sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 shall apply to applications and appeals under this rule. *****************

sections.title: CHAPTER V - E-FILING PROCEDURE [1] As parts of the efforts to employ technology...
sections.text: CHAPTER V - E-FILING PROCEDURE [1] As parts of the efforts to employ technology to expediate court proceedings, filing of cases through electronic mode has been introduced in the High Court by the enactment of the Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala) 2021, hereinafter referred to as the E-Filing Rules. Only a brief summary of the Rules is extracted below for general guidance. [2] As per Rule 2(b) of the E-Filing Rules Action means all proceedings instituted in the court whether fresh, pending and disposed which shall be filed electronically by the E-Filer in the manner provided in Rule 3(3) of the E-Filing Rules. Online electronic filing shall be made in the High Court by visiting the web portal of the High Court or that is assigned specifically for electronic filing by the Chief Justice. [3] A pleading as defined in Rule 2(w) of the E-Filing Rules shall be prepared electronically using any word processing software [see Rule 5(1) E-Filing Rules]. The following format shall be followed for [i] Pleadings: The pleadings filed should strictly confirm to the requirements as prescribed in the relevant Acts and Rules [see Rule 5(7) E-Filing Rules]. The pleadings shall be prepared on A-4 size paper. The Font of the letters shall be Times New Roman and the typeface shall be 14 points. A document that is to be typed in the local language of the Court shall be typed using UNICODE Font 12. All text shall be of 1.5 line spaced and all documents shall alignment with justified alignment. The top margin shall be 1.5”; Bottom Margin 1.5”; Left Margin 1.75” and the Right Margin 1.0”. The pleadings and the documents produced in support of the pleadings shall be converted in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) searchable PDF or PDF/A document. [ii] Documents other than text documents: When the document is not a text document and has to be enclosed along with the pleadings, the document shall be scanned using an image resolution of 300 DPI (Dots Per Inch) in OCR searchable mode and saved as a PDF or PDF/A. The E-Filer shall ensure that the documents are an accurate representation of the document and is complete and readable. When the original of the document is not clearly legible, a typed copy of the document duly certified by the Advocate or Party-in-Person shall also be scanned and uploaded along with the original [see Rule 5(5) E- Filing Rules]. When the documents produced along with the pleadings or subsequently produced is not the original of the document, then the Advocate or the Party-in-Person producing the document, shall endorse on the top of the first page of the document, that the document is not the original document and that it is only a certified copy or a photocopy of the original document. [See Rule 5(6) E-Filing Rules] [4] Authentication of documents: An electronically filed document shall be authenticated in either of the following manners as provided in Rule 6 of the E-Filing Rules Authentication using Digital Signature of the advocate or party-in-person: The digital signature shall be affixed on such places as are mandated under the relevant Acts and Rules. Adhaar authentication using his Adhaar number and the OTP sent to the registered number of the Advocate or Party-in-person: Where the advocate or party-in-person do not possess the digital signature as issued by competent authority, such authentication shall be considered as a valid identification for all intents and purposes. Electronic Mail Address (e-mail) or mobile phone number-based OTP authentication: An advocate or party-in-person who does not possess the digital signature or electronic signature, can authenticate electronically filed documents in this method.

sections.title: Authentication by Physical signature: Where authentication in any of the...
sections.text:
Authentication by Physical signature: Where authentication in any of the above-mentioned methods is not possible, a print out of the pleadings or documents shall be physically signed in accordance with the relevant rules and thereafter it shall be scanned and uploaded. [5] Scrutiny of E- filed documents: The Registry shall on scrutiny of the pleadings or documents filed, note the objections regarding the non-compliance with the Rules or Practice Directions or any other law for the time being in force. These objections shall be informed to the E-filer through electronic mail or any other electronic mode. The E-filer shall cure the defects within the time provided and return the Efiled pleadings and documents within the time provided. [See Rule 17 E-Filing Rules] [6] Limitation: E-filer shall file all actions within the prescribed limitation period. (Rule 13 (1) of the Rules). The date of electronic filing for computation of the period of limitation shall be taken as the date when the Action is electronically received in the Registry within the time [Indian Standard Time] prescribed under the relevant Act/Rules and orders issued from time to time. [See Rule 13 (1) & (2) E-Filing Rules) [7] Service through electronic means: The Court may serve the pleadings and documents that are electronically filed to the user account of the E-Filer through the designated electronic file system user account of the Registry or to his electronic mail account or through electronic post [e-post] or through any other electronic mode as prescribed by the Court. The same shall be in addition to the prescribed mode of service as per the relevant Acts and Rules. [See Rule 11(1) E-Filing Rules] A person facing an action shall be entitled to make a written application to the concerned Registry to provide him with the hard copy of the pleadings or documents filed. The Registry, on being satisfied that sufficient reasons are made out in the written application, shall then direct the person who initiated the Action either to provide the hard copy of the pleadings or documents or to deposit the charges required for taking photocopy of the same. [See Rule 17
(6) of the E-Filing Rules] [8] Party in person: A Party-in-Person who institutes or defends an Action shall submit an affidavit or an undertaking stating that he has not engaged an Advocate in the Action. [See Rule 3(6) of the E-Filing Rules] ***********************

sections.title: CHAPTER VI - AFFIDAVITS FILED IN THE HIGH COURT [1] Chapter VI of the “Rules” -...
sections.chapter_title: Affidavits Filed In The High Court
sections.text:
CHAPTER VI - AFFIDAVITS FILED IN THE HIGH COURT [1] Chapter VI of the “Rules” - Rule 72 to Rule 84 deals with Affidavits filed in the High Court along with the main proceedings. Form Nos. 4; 5; 6; and 7 of the “Rules” prescribe the form of Affidavit of solemn affirmation; Certification when deponent is unacquainted with the language of the affidavit or is blind or illiterate; Certificate to be endorsed on an exhibit to an affidavit and concluding portion of affidavit respectively. The important rules are mentioned herein: Heading of affidavits. - Every affidavit shall be entitled “In the High Court of Kerala” and shall set forth the cause title of the appeal or other matter in which the affidavit is sought to be filed. An affidavit in support of, or in opposition to, an interlocutory application relating to a pending appeal, petition or other proceeding shall also be entitled as made in such appeal, petition or other proceeding. Form of affidavit. - Every affidavit shall be drawn up in the first person and be divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively; and each paragraph, as nearly as may be, shall be confined to a distinct portion of the subject matter. Contents of affidavits. - Every affidavit shall state the full name, age, description and place of abode of the deponent, and shall be signed or marked by him. Where the affidavit covers more than one page, the deponent shall sign every page. The description shall include the father’s or Karnavan’s or husband’s or mother’s name and such other particulars as may be necessary to identify the person Alterations, erasures etc.– Alterations, erasures and interlineations shall, before an affidavit is sworn or affirmed, be authenticated by the persons before whom the affidavit is signed, and no affidavit having therein any alteration, erasure or interlineation not so authenticated, shall, except with the leave of the Court, be filed or made use of in any manner. Persons authenticating affidavits. – Affidavits may be sworn or affirmed before any Judicial Officer, a District Registrar or Sub Registrar, the Chief Ministerial Officer of any Civil or Criminal Court in the State of Kerala, a member of Parliament or of the Legislature of any State in India, the Mayor, Chairman, President, Executive Authority or a member of any Municipal Corporation, Municipal Council or other Local Authority in India, a Gazetted Officer serving in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State in India, a Commissioned Officer in the Defence Forces in India, or an Advocate. Mode of authentication. - The person before whom an affidavit is sworn or affirmed shall state the date on which, and the place where the same is made, and sign under his name and designation at the end as in Form No.4 Blind or illiterate deponent.- Where an affidavit is sworn or affirmed by any person who appears to the person authenticating the affidavit to be illiterate, blind or unacquainted with the language in which the affidavit is written, the person authenticating shall certify that the affidavit was read, explained or translated by him or in his presence to the deponent, that the deponent seemed to understand it, and made his signature or mark in the presence of the authenticating as is in Form No.5 Identification of deponent. - (1) If the deponent of an affidavit is not known to the person authenticating the same, the identity of the deponent shall be caused to be testified by any person known to him, who shall attest the signature or mark of the deponent in token thereof.
(2) Where the deponent is a pardanashin lady she shall be identified by a person to whom she is known and that person shall verify the identification by a separate affidavit. Documents referred to in affidavits. – Documents mentioned in and accompanying an affidavit shall be referred to as exhibits and shall be marked in the same manner as exhibits and shall bear a certificate as in Form No.6 signed by the person before whom the affidavit is sworn or affirmed. Affidavit stating opinion. - Every affidavit stating any matter of opinion shall show the qualification of the deponent to express such opinion, by reference to the length of experience, acquaintance, with the person or matter as to which the opinion is expressed or other means of knowledge of the deponent. Affidavit on information and belief. - Every affidavit shall clearly express how much is a statement of the deponent’s knowledge and how much is statement of his belief, as in Form No.7.

sections.title: The grounds of belief must be stated with sufficient particularity to enable...
sections.chapter_title: Affidavits Filed In The High Court
sections.text: The grounds of belief must be stated with sufficient particularity to enable the Court to judge whether it would be safe to act on the dependent’s belief. Filing of affidavits in Court. - Except with the leave of the Court, no affidavit which has not been filed in Court and of which copy has not been given to the other parties at least three days before the hearing shall be used in any manner. Counter affidavits. - The parties to whom copies of affidavits have been given shall be entitled to file counter affidavits, copies of which shall be given to the remaining parties, who may, if they choose, file further affidavits in reply, but, except with the leave of the Court, no further affidavits shall be filed. [2] AFFIDAVITS IN PUBLIC INTEREST LITIGATION Special requirement for affidavits accompanying Public Interest Litigations is mandated under Rule 146A of the “Rules”. Rule146 A Affidavits in Public Interest Litigations .- A person filing a public interest litigation in addition to the requirements stipulated in the other rules of this chapter shall precisely and specifically affirm in the affidavit to be sworn by him the public cause he is seeking to espouse, that he has no personal or private interest in the matter, that there is no authoritative pronouncement by the Supreme Court or the High Court on the question raised and that the result of the litigation shall not lead to any undue gain to himself or to anyone associated with him. Official Memorandum Non-permission of corrections and interpolations in the affidavits filed before the High Court – It has been noticed that the affidavit filed along with the I.A.No.208/2011 in COC No.178/2011 of the Hon’ble Court, contained material corrections by way of interpolations made by the counsel. While scrutiny, the above defect was not noted by the Examiner concerned and the case was posted before the Bench. The Hon’ble the Chief Justice, having noticed the defect, has ordered that appropriate instructions be issued to the officers concerned. All concerned are hereby instructed to see that affidavits do not contain any corrections or interlineations. If there are any minor corrections, they should be authenticated by the deponent. Affidavits with defects shall not be accepted unless otherwise directed by the Hon’ble Court. Official Memorandum No.A6-32219/2011 dt.23.5.2011 issued by the High Court ************************

sections.title: CHAPTER VII - SERVICE OF NOTICES [1] Chapter IV of the “Rules” – Rule 51 to...
sections.text:
CHAPTER VII - SERVICE OF NOTICES [1] Chapter IV of the “Rules” – Rule 51 to Rule 68 – exhaustively deal with service of notices. Rule 57 of the “Rules” states that the process fee levied shall be at the rates prescribed from time to time under the Court Fees Act. The present rate of process fees levied is given in Chapter XXIV of this book. [2] Rule 51 of the “Rules” prescribes the manner of issue of notice; Rule 51A prescribes the service of notice on any adult member of the family, whether male or female, who is residing with the respondent, in case the respondent is absent from his residence at the time when the service is sought to be effected on him; Rule 51B prescribes the mode in which the notice can be served by affixing and Rule 51C prescribes the service of notice by substituted service. [3] Rule 63 of the “Rules” states that unless otherwise ordered by the court or provided for otherwise by the “Rules”, when notice has been ordered, the party shall pay the prescribed fees for service of notice within three days after the date of order and that the interim order made upon the application shall not be issued until the prescribed fees have been paid. [4] Rule 59 of the “Rules” also provide for serving the notice of proceeding instituted in the High Court on the Pleader appearing in the Subordinate Court. Service of notice on the Pleader in the Subordinate Court.- (1) In an appeal from preliminary decree or in any appeal, or other proceeding instituted in the High Court before the disposal of the main proceeding in the Subordinate Court, notice may be served on the pleader who represents the party in the proceeding in the Subordinate Court and such service shall be deemed to be sufficient service on the party who is represented by such pleader. Where a party is not represented by a pleader in the main proceeding, notice shall be served on the party direct.
(2) Whereas the pleader on record for a party declines to receive such notice, the case shall be posted before court for orders. [5] Electronic Service of Notice Rule 11 of the Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala), 2021 enables the court to serve notice through user account of an E-filer or through e-mail, e-post or such other electronic means as prescribed by the Court and the same shall be in addition to the prescribed means of service in the relevant Acts and Rules Case Laws: Declaration of Notice – As per the second proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 51 of the High Court Rules no declaration that notice has been duly served on the respondent shall be made if the postal article containing the notice is received back by the Court with an endorsement purporting to have been made by a postal employee to the effect that the address has not claimed it. Kalliani & others Vs Shibu v & others 2019 (4) KLT 436 Notice to advocate appearing before Subordinate Court in Criminal Proceedings - Notice given to an Advocate appearing for the respondent in a Criminal Proceedings pending before the Subordinate Court can be reckoned as a sufficient notice on such respondent of the proceedings initiated before the High Court. The Advocate who receives the notice is bound to inform his client of the pendency of the proceedings before the High Court. Geetha Panciker v Lagi Easo Mathew 2003(3) KLT 454 Declaration of service of notice – Declaration of service of notice can be made only by the Court and not by the Registry of the Court. Matter to be posted before the bench for orders. Leela Mathew v Krishnamoorthy 2007(3) KLT 867

sections.title: Service of summons/notice/judicial process on persons residing abroad – No...
sections.text: Service of summons/notice/judicial process on persons residing abroad – No notice/summons can be sent directly to a person residing in a foreign country which is party to Hague Convention 1965. [In this judgment, the Hon’ble Court has extracted in detail the General Procedure formulated by the Registry of the Court to be followed for service of notice in civil and commercial matters, on persons residing abroad.] Mollykutty @ Mollykutty Vallant v Nicey Jacob & other 2019(3) KHC 118 DB Official Memorandum Comprehensive Guidelines for investigation abroad and issue of Letter Rogatory (LRs)/Mutual Legal Assistance (MLA) Request and Service of Summons/Notices/Judicial documents in respect of Criminal Matters- The High Court vide references (1) High Court O.M.D1B-21216/2009 dt.12.05.2009 (2) High Court O.M.D3- 66559/2018 dt.22.06.2019 had issued comprehensive guidelines regarding the service of summons, notice and judicial process on persons residing in foreign countries to all the Subordinate Courts in the State and all Sections on the Judicial side of the High Court. Now, the Ministry of Home Affairs has forwarded revised guidelines in respect of Letter Rogatory (LRs), Mutual Legal Assistance (MLA) request and service of summons/notices/judicial documents etc. abroad, incorporating various legal and technical developments in the recent years with an aim to make the documentation in this regard more precise and focused as well as complaint with international requirements. The said Comprehensive Guidelines for investigation abroad and issue of Letter Rogatory (LRs)/Mutual Legal Assistance (MLA) Request and Service of Summons/Notices/Judicial documents in respect of criminal matters are available under the link: https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/ISII_ComprehensiveGuidelines16032020.pdf Official Memorandum No.D1-3/2345/2020 dt.01.02.2020 issued by the High Court ************************

sections.title: CHAPTER VIII - APPOINTMENT OF GUARDIAN [1] Chapter V – Rule 69 to Rule 71 of...
sections.text: CHAPTER VIII - APPOINTMENT OF GUARDIAN [1] Chapter V – Rule 69 to Rule 71 of the “Rules” deals with the procedure to be followed while appointing a Guardian for a minor respondent. The provisions contained in Order XXXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 which deal with Suits by or against Minors and Persons of Unsound Mind has also to be referred to. Guardian Application. - Every application for the appointment of guardian for a minor respondent shall be supported by an affidavit stating that the proposed guardian has no interest in any matter in question in the proceeding adverse to that of the minor. No order shall be made on the application unless notice thereof has been duly served upon the father or guardian of the minor or upon the person with whom the minor resides, 7 clear days before the day named in the notice for the hearing of the application. Application not to be combined with application to bring on record legal representatives. - An application for the appointment of a guardian ad litem shall not be combined with an application for bringing on record the legal representatives of a deceased appellant petitioner or respondent. Provision of funds.- When a guardian ad litem of a minor respondent is appointed, and it appears to the Court that the guardian is not in possession of any or sufficient funds for the conduct of the case on behalf of the respondent, and that the respondent will be prejudiced in his defence thereby, the Court may, from time to time, order the appellant or petitioner to advance moneys to the guardian for the purpose of his defence, and all moneys so advanced shall form part of the costs of the appellant or the petitioner. The order may direct that the guardian do, as and when directed, file in Court an account of the money so received by him. *****************

sections.title: CHAPTER IX - CERTIFIED COPY OF JUDGMENT & RECORDS [1] Chapter X of the “Rules”...
sections.text: CHAPTER IX - CERTIFIED COPY OF JUDGMENT & RECORDS [1] Chapter X of the “Rules” – Rules 128 to 138 – deals with the procedure to be followed for getting certified copies of judgement, orders and copy of proceedings or documents filed in the custody of the court. [2] Rule 128 of the “Rules” states that any application for obtaining a certified copy of any proceeding or judgment or document filed in or in the custody of the Court, shall be filed in Form No.9, either in person or by online process after paying the requisite fees prescribed under Rule 137 by electronic payment (e-payment). As per Rule 137 of the “Rules” the copying charges shall be fixed by the Chief Justice from time to time which shall be notified and published in the official website of the High Court of Kerala. [3] Rule 131 of the Rules provides for the application for Copies by a Party to the Proceedings in the High Court and Rule 132 of the “Rules” provide for application for Copies by Persons not Party to the Proceedings. Rule 133 of the “Rules” states that records of documents filed in subordinate courts which forms part of the case records pending in the High Court, if they are available in the High Court, a certified copy of the record can be obtained from the High Court on the orders of the Registrar (Judicial) on filing a duly verified petition setting forth the necessity and the reason as to why the copy was not obtained from the Subordinate Court. Rule 135 states that the authorised officer shall intimate the date for appearance to receive the copy in the e-mail address of the applicant and also notify the date for appearance on the notice board in the section. Rule 138 (4) states that the certified copy can also be issued in digitized form in the manner as may be prescribed from time to time by the Chief Justice. [4] The High Court vide notification dated 18.5.2020 has made facility for availing the certified copy of the judgment and orders through online process. Certified Copy – Online Process -Copy of judgments and orders issued by the High Court shall be applied invariably through online mode via the web address https://ecourts.kerala.gov.in. The delivery of certified copies in digitized form shall also be made in online mode. Facility is also made for payment of requisite fees digitally. The charges for certified copies in physical form shall be realised as per the existing rules. The charges for issuing certified copies online are: a) for judgments: Rs.50/- per copy b) for orders: Rs.30/- per copy Notification No: DI-1/20613/2018 dt:18.05.2020 issued by the High Court **********************

CHAPTER X - PECUNIARY JURISDICTION OF CIVIL COURTS AND HIGH COURT [1] Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957 The Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to civil courts in the State of Kerala, subordinate to the High Court of Kerala. The said Act has undergone amendments regarding the pecuniary jurisdiction, the last being in the year 2013. As per this amendment, sub-section (2) of Section 11 and sub-section (1) of Section 13 of the Kerala Civil Courts Act were amended with effect from 6.5.2013. Amendment of Section 11 In sub-section (2) of Section 11 of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957, for the words "one lakh rupees", the words "ten lakh rupees" shall be substituted. Amendment of Section 13 In sub-section (1) of Section 13 of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957, for the words "two lakh rupees", the words “twenty lakh rupees” shall be substituted. The relevant provisions of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957 are extracted below: Section 11 Section 12 Section 13 Jurisdiction of District Court and Subordinate Judge’s Court in original suits. - (1) The Jurisdiction of a District Court or a Subordinate Judge’s Court extends, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908(5 of 1908) to all original suits and proceedings of civil nature.
(2) The jurisdiction of a Munsiff’s Court extends to all like suits and proceedings not otherwise exempted from its cognizance of which the amount of value of the subject-matter does not exceed ten lakh rupees. Appeals from decrees and order of District Court or Subordinate Judge’s Court. - Save as provided in Section 13, regular and special appeals shall, when such appeals are allowed by law, lie from the decrees or orders of a District Court or a Subordinate Judge’s Court to the High Court. Appellate Jurisdiction of District Court and Subordinate Judge’s Court. -
(1) Appeals from the decrees and order of a Munsiff’s Court and where the amount or value of the subject matter of the suit does not exceed twenty lakh rupees from the original decrees and orders of a Subordinate Judge’s Court shall, when such appeals are allowed by law, lie to the District Court:
Provided that whenever a Subordinate Judge’s Court is established in any district at a place other than the place where the District Court is stationed, appeals from the decrees or orders of the Munsiff’s Courts within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such Subordinate Judge’s Court may be preferred in such Subordinate Judge’s Court:
Provided further that the District Court may remove to itself from time to time appeals so preferred and dispose of them itself or may, subject to the orders of the High Court, refer any appeals from the decrees and orders of Munsiff’s Courts preferred in the District Court to any Subordinate Judge’s Court within the district.
(2) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall apply to original decrees and orders of a Subordinate Judge’s Courts passed after the commencement of the Kerala Civil Courts (Amendment) Act, 1959, notwithstanding the fact that the suits in respect of which such decrees and orders have been passed were instituted before such commencement. [2] Kerala High Court Act, 1958 Section 3(13)(b) of the Kerala High Court Act, 1958 prescribes the pecuniary jurisdiction of Single Judge in hearing an appeal from an original decree or order in any suit or other proceedings. Case Laws: Suit instituted and decreed before amendment – Effect of amendment – Proper forum for appeal – The right of appeal is a substantive right and not a mere matter of procedure and the institution of the suit carries with it the implication that all rights of appeal then in force are preserved to the parties till the rest of the career of the suit. This vested right of appeal can be taken away only by a subsequent enactment if it so provides expressly or by necessary intendment and not otherwise. Clara v Augustine ILR 1984(2) Ker 498 DB Valuation of suit decides the forum of appeal. - Jurisdiction of the appellate court is decided on the basis of Section 13 of the Civil Courts Act and not on the basis of Section 52 of the Court Fees Act. For the purpose of jurisdiction, valuation of the suit is relevant. The forum of Appeal is decided on the basis of the valuation of the suit. Valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction and for the purpose of court fee need not be the same. That is the indication in Section 53 of the Court Fees Act. Valuation of the suit is static and it decides the forum of appeal. If the valuation for the purpose of court fee is taken as the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction in cases where specific provision is made in the Court Fees for the valuation of a suit, anomalous situations may arise. CHAPTER XII - PROCEEDINGS UNDER ARTICLE 226; 227 & 228 OF CONSTITUTION OF INDIA [1] Constitution of India Article226 Article227 Article228 Power of High Courts to issue certain writs. —
(1) Notwithstanding anything in Article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
(2) The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power, notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories.
(3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—(a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and(b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard, makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated.
(4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32. Power of superintendence over all courts by the High Court. -
(1) Every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.
(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the High Court may—(a) call for returns from such courts; (b) make and issue general rules and prescribe forms for regulating the practice and proceedings of such courts; and(c) prescribe forms in which books, entries and accounts shall be kept by the officers of any such courts
(3) The High Court may also settle tables of fees to be allowed to the sheriff and all clerks and officers of such courts and to attorneys, advocates and pleaders practising therein:
Provided that any rules made, forms prescribed or tables settled under clause (2) or clause (3) shall not be inconsistent with the provision of any law for the time being in force, and shall require the previous approval of the Governor.
(4) Nothing in this article shall be deemed to confer on a High Court power of superintendence over any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces. Transfer of certain cases to High Court. - If the High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, it shall withdraw the case and may—(a) either dispose of the case itself, or(b) determine the said question of law and return the case to the court from which the case has been so withdrawn together with a copy of its judgment on such question, and the said court shall on receipt thereof proceed to dispose of the case in conformity with such judgment.

Interim orders. - (1) In admitting the application, it shall be competent for the Court to pass interim order on motion made for the same so as to meet the ends of justice.
(2) Any motion for interim relief at the time of admission may be made in the application under Article 226 or 227 or 228 of the Constitution itself in the relief portion:

Provided further that no petition shall be entertained by the Registry unless it contains a statement as to whether the petitioner had filed any petition seeking similar reliefs in respect of the same subject matter earlier and if so, the results thereof. Process Fees. - Except in the case of a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus, the petitioner shall pay the necessary process fee for service of notices and orders on the respondents. sections.title: [iii] Copy of the Writ Petition, Counter Affidavits, Reply Affidavits etc....
sections.text: [iii] Copy of the Writ Petition, Counter Affidavits, Reply Affidavits etc. produced in the Writ Petition has to be produced along with the Writ Appeal. [iv] For the Advocate who had appeared in the Writ Petition, no fresh vakalath is necessary. Only a memo of appearance need be filed. Case Laws: Cross objection in Writ Appeals- Cross objection under Order XLI Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is not maintainable in a Writ Appeal filed under Section 5 of the Kerala High Court Act. Provisions of Order 41 Rule 22 of the C.P.Code as regards cross objection cannot be made applicable to proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. George J v State of Kerala & others ILR 2019(3) Ker 475 DB Duty of Registry to send the unnumbered case to bench if party or counsel requires the maintainability to be adjudicated by the Court- Even though Registry is free to consider maintainability and are free to record reason and refuse to number the same without orders from Bench, if party or counsel filing the case requires maintainability to be adjudicated by the Court on the judicial side, it is the duty of the Registry to send the unnumbered case to the concerned Judge or Court. Ayub Khan P.A. v State of Kerala ILR 2012(1) Ker 615 DB Court Fee in Writ Appeals under Rule 159(2) of the “Rules”– Appeal filed by three representatives of SNDP Yogam which is a charitable trust and all of them claiming a single right on behalf of the Yogam – The three appellants are not claiming any right to relief of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions jointly or severally. If they were doing so, then they would have become liable to pay court-fee of Rs.100/- each [now Rs.200/-] in accordance with the latter part of Rule 159(2). Narayanan Ragavan v Noordeen ILR 1993(3) Ker 543 DB Court Fee payable in a Writ Appeal filed by legal representatives of a deceased writ petitioner jointly - When a pending litigation is pursued by the legal heirs of a writ petitioner, they need not pay separate court fee since the predecessor in interest has already paid the court fee. In the event of such matter being pursued in Writ Appeal by all the legal heirs jointly, they need only pay one set of court fee in the appeal. But if there is difference of opinion among the legal heirs and the legal heirs choose to file separate Writ Appeals, either in groups or individually then those groups will have to pay one set of court fee each and if the Writ Appeal is filed individually, each individual will have to pay the court fee at the prescribed rate. Eliyamma Kuriakose & others v Plantation Corporation of Kerala Ltd. & another ILR 2010(1) Ker266 DB Writ Petition filed by Association having several members; court fee payable. - Writ Petition filed by Association having several members. Since all of the persons in the Association are interested persons court fee has to be paid at the rate of Rs.100/- per person under the provisions of Schedule II Article 11(l) (iii) of Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959 [See Rule 147A Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971] Maradu Market Trader’s Association v State of Kerala & others 2018(3) KLT 212 DB Writ Petition filed by a society registered under the Travancore-Cochin Literary, Scientific & Charitable Societies Registration Act 1955; whether court fee has to be paid for all the members of the Association. - In the light of Section 9 of the T.C. Literary, Scientific & Charitable Societies Registration Act, a writ petition instituted by a society registered under the T.C.Act of 1955 for the benefit of its members cannot be treated as a writ petition instituted by its members jointly and the petitioner Society cannot be insisted to remit court fee for all its members. I take this view also for the reason that if the legislature had intended to levy court fee on all members of an association registered under the Act in a matter like this, it would have certainly made a provision for the same in the Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959.Coming to the order in Maradu Market Trader’s Association v State of Kerala & others 2018(3) KLT 212 DB the said case being one instituted by an unregistered association, this court was certainly justified in directing the petitioner to pay court fee for all its members placing reliance on Rule 147A of the Rules of the High Court of Kerala and therefore, the said order cannot be an impediment in taking the view aforesaid. Association of LPG Distributors in Kerala v Indian Oil Corporation 2021(5) KLT 429

sections.title: State Government Party - Where State Government is a party, Secretary to the...
sections.text: State Government Party - Where State Government is a party, Secretary to the concerned department shall be arrayed as a respondent – If the subject matter of the petition relates to two or more Government Departments, Chief Secretary to Government and Secretaries to those Government Departments shall be made a party representing Government Sobhana v Panavally Grama Panchayath & others ILR 2019 (3) Ker 722 Facts Not Verified - Facts stated and allegations made in accordance to law in the writ petition not verified, which is in turn fatal to the writ petition. Joveson C.J. & another v Chief Justice of Kerala High Court & others ILR 2018[2] Ker 917 Additional Documents Produced – If petitioner wants to rely on certain additional facts or additional documents, he has to file an interlocutory application under Rule 154, which should be supported by an affidavit sworn to by the petitioner. Kunjalavi Chellamma v District Geologist, Dept. of Mining Geology, Kollam & others 2016 (4) KLT 293 Whether necessary to state petitioner or respondent - Unnecessary for a person invoking Rule 152 of the Rules of the High Court of Kerala to state specifically as to whether he seeks impleadment in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution, as a petitioner or as a respondent. Nalan P.K. & another v D.Vinesh & others 2009 (4) KLT 784 Affidavit to contain clear statement in proof of facts - Affidavit filed in support of writ petition shall contain clear statements in proof of the facts stated in the writ petition and also in proof of documents tendered along with the writ petition. If the original of the document is not in the possession of the petitioner and yet he is in possession of a copy which he believes to be true and which is required to be tendered along with Writ Petition, he has to state so in his affidavit, as also the source of the copy and as to whether he believes that its contents are true Siddique v District Collector ILR 2006(3) Ker 731 Whether any affected party can file a Writ Appeal – A person cannot seek leave to prefer a Writ Appeal against the judgment passed by a learned Judge dismissing a Writ Petition filed by a person similar to him. His remedy is to file a Writ Petition. Sabeesh v Jyothi Kumar 2006 (3) KLT 710 DB Stranger cannot be impleaded as petitioner - A stranger cannot be allowed to be added as one of the petitioners after the Writ Petition under Article 226 is already filed. Order 1 Rule 10(2) of C.P.Code, 1908 cannot be applied. Karassery Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. v State of Kerala &others 2020 KHC 572 Vijayan & others v Commr. Corporation of Cochin & others 1987(1) KLT 665 Court fee to be paid by Legal Heirs- When the heirs of a deceased person files a Writ Petition as a legal entity, only a court fee of Rs.25/- [now Rs.100/-] need be paid. Appa v State of Kerala 1980 KLT 717 “As directed by Court” not to be insisted by Registry - If an application is filed for a particular purpose, the Registry is expected to see that the application is in proper form and proper court fee is paid. It is for the court to decide whether the application is to be allowed or not. The Registry shall not insist on writing on the application “as directed by the Court” when there was no such direction by the Court. If the Registry feels that the application is not maintainable unless there was a specific direction by the Court in that regard, the Registry is free to return the application as defective, so that the party concerned may answer. Unless there is a specific direction by the Court, no party is entitled to mention in the application that it is filed “as directed by the Court.” Sarada T.A. & others v Jayan & others ILR 2012(4) Ker 729 DB Additional Evidence in Writ Appeals - In writ appeals there has to be an application under Order 41 Rule 27 C.P.Code for admission of additional evidence in terms of that provision by producing documents supported by an affidavit and duly certified/authenticated in terms of Rule 147(2) of the “Rules” Special Tahsildar (LA) & others v P.C.Mathew ILR 2013(3) Ker 628 DB
